description: This topic explains the meaning and functions of political parties, the difference between one-party and multi-party systems, Tanzania's 1992 return to multipartyism, and the role of pressure groups, civil society and the media in a democracy.

options.text: A group of people who organise to win government power and put their policies into action
A government department that collects taxes
A private company that sells goods for profit
A court that settles disputes between citizens

mcq.explanation: A political party is an organised group of people who share similar ideas and aim to gain control of government through elections in order to implement their policies.

mcq.questionText: In which year did Tanzania officially return to a multi-party political system?
mcq.explanation: Tanzania ended its one-party system and reintroduced multipartyism in 1992 after the constitution was amended to allow more than one political party.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a key function of a political party in a democracy?

options.text: Educating citizens politically and mobilising them to participate in elections

mcq.explanation: Political parties educate the public about issues and policies, and they mobilise citizens to vote and take part in political life.

mcq.questionText: A one-party system is a system in which:

options.text: Only one political party is legally allowed to operate and contest for power
Many parties freely compete in elections
There are no elections at all

mcq.explanation: In a one-party (single-party) system, the law permits only one party to exist and compete for power, as Tanzania experienced from 1965 until 1992.

mcq.questionText: Which institution is responsible for registering political parties in Tanzania?

options.text: The Office of the Registrar of Political Parties

mcq.explanation: The Office of the Registrar of Political Parties is the body that registers parties and ensures they follow the laws governing parties in Tanzania.

mcq.questionText: What is the main role of an opposition party in a democracy?

options.text: To rule the country without elections
To check the government, offer alternative policies and hold leaders accountable

mcq.explanation: The opposition scrutinises the ruling party, criticises poor decisions, suggests alternative policies and helps keep the government accountable to the people.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best describes a pressure group?

options.text: An organisation that seeks to win government power through elections
A group that tries to influence government decisions on specific issues without seeking to form a government
A branch of the armed forces
A part of the national parliament

mcq.explanation: Pressure groups aim to influence policy on particular interests or issues; unlike political parties, they do not contest elections to form a government.

mcq.questionText: What is the main difference between a political party and a pressure group?

options.text: A political party seeks to form the government, while a pressure group seeks only to influence it
A pressure group is bigger than every political party
A political party is illegal while a pressure group is legal
There is no difference between them

mcq.explanation: Political parties want to capture government power, whereas pressure groups only want to influence government policy on chosen issues.

mcq.questionText: Which of these is an example of a civil society organisation?

options.text: A non-governmental organisation (NGO) that promotes human rights

mcq.explanation: Civil society organisations such as NGOs operate independently of government and work on issues like human rights, health, education and development.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a role of the media in a democracy?

options.text: To inform citizens and expose wrongdoing so leaders can be held accountable

mcq.explanation: A free media keeps citizens informed, gives them a platform to express views, and acts as a watchdog by exposing corruption and abuse of power.

options.text: Protect and promote the rights and welfare of workers

mcq.explanation: Trade unions are a type of pressure group that defend workers' interests, such as fair wages and good working conditions.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an advantage of a multi-party system?

options.text: It removes the need for elections
It gives citizens a choice of leaders and policies and allows peaceful competition for power
It guarantees that no one criticises the government

mcq.explanation: A multi-party system widens citizens' choices, encourages accountability through competition, and allows power to change hands peacefully.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a possible disadvantage of a multi-party system?

options.text: It can create division and conflict if competition becomes too bitter

mcq.explanation: Strong competition between parties can sometimes lead to tension, division along ethnic or regional lines, and wasted resources during campaigns.

mcq.questionText: Faith-based organisations contribute to democracy mainly by:

options.text: Promoting peace, moral values and social services and speaking out on justice

mcq.explanation: Religious organisations often promote peace and moral values, provide schools and hospitals, and advocate for justice and good governance.

mcq.questionText: Why is citizen participation important in a democracy?

options.text: Because it allows the government to ignore the people
Because it ensures that government reflects the will of the people and remains accountable
Because it ends all political parties
Because it stops people from voting

mcq.explanation: When citizens participate by voting, debating and joining organisations, the government better reflects their wishes and can be held accountable.

fib.questionText: An organised group that seeks to win government power and implement its policies is called a political _____.
fib.explanation: A political party organises people who share ideas to compete for and exercise government power.

fib.questionText: Tanzania returned to a multi-party system in the year _____.
fib.explanation: The constitution was amended in 1992 to allow more than one political party in Tanzania.

fib.questionText: A system in which only one party is legally allowed to operate is called a _____-party system.
fib.explanation: A one-party (single-party) system permits only one party to compete for power.

fib.questionText: Political parties in Tanzania are registered by the Office of the Registrar of Political _____.
fib.explanation: The Office of the Registrar of Political Parties registers parties and oversees the rules they must follow.

fib.questionText: A group that tries to influence government decisions without seeking to form a government is called a _____ group.
fib.explanation: Pressure groups influence policy on specific issues but do not contest elections to form a government.

fib.questionText: Organisations that defend workers' rights and welfare are called trade _____.
fib.explanation: Trade unions are pressure groups that protect the interests of workers.

fib.questionText: The party that checks the government and offers alternative policies is known as the _____.
fib.explanation: The opposition scrutinises the ruling party and holds it accountable.

fib.questionText: Non-governmental organisations and other independent groups that work for public good are together called civil _____ organisations.
fib.explanation: Civil society organisations operate independently of government to serve community interests.

fib.questionText: Because it informs the public and exposes wrongdoing, the free media is often called the _____ of society.
fib.explanation: The media acts as a watchdog that monitors leaders and exposes abuse of power.

fib.questionText: When citizens vote, debate and join organisations, they are taking part in political _____.
fib.explanation: Citizen participation keeps government responsive and accountable to the people.

tf.questionText: A political party aims to win government power and put its policies into practice.
tf.explanation: Seeking and exercising government power to implement policies is the defining aim of a political party.

tf.questionText: Tanzania has always been a multi-party state since independence in 1961.
tf.explanation: Tanzania operated as a one-party state for many years and only returned to multipartyism in 1992.

tf.questionText: In a one-party system, only one political party is legally allowed to contest for power.
tf.explanation: A one-party system by definition allows only a single legal party.

tf.questionText: The opposition's role is to support every government decision without question.
tf.explanation: The opposition's role is to check the government and offer alternatives, not to agree with everything.

tf.questionText: Pressure groups normally contest elections to form the national government.
tf.explanation: Unlike political parties, pressure groups only try to influence policy and do not seek to form a government.

tf.questionText: The Office of the Registrar of Political Parties registers parties in Tanzania.
tf.explanation: This office is responsible for registering political parties and ensuring they obey the law.

tf.questionText: Trade unions and faith-based organisations are examples of civil society.
tf.explanation: Trade unions, religious bodies and NGOs are all part of civil society working outside government.

tf.questionText: A free and responsible media helps citizens make informed decisions.
tf.explanation: By providing accurate information, the media enables citizens to judge leaders and policies wisely.

tf.questionText: A multi-party system has only advantages and no disadvantages.
tf.explanation: While it offers choice and accountability, a multi-party system can also bring division and high campaign costs.

tf.questionText: Citizen participation strengthens democracy by keeping government accountable.
tf.explanation: Active participation ensures leaders serve the people and remain answerable to them.

summary.correctAnswer: A political party is an organised group of people who share similar ideas and seek to win government power through elections in order to implement their policies.
summary.explanation: This captures the shared ideas, organisation and aim of gaining power that define a party.

summary.questionText: List three functions of political parties.
summary.correctAnswer: Educating citizens politically, mobilising people to vote, selecting candidates and forming or checking the government.
summary.explanation: Parties perform political education, mobilisation, candidate selection and either governing or opposing.

summary.questionText: Explain the difference between a one-party and a multi-party system.
summary.correctAnswer: In a one-party system only one party is legally allowed, while in a multi-party system many parties freely compete for power in elections.
summary.explanation: The key difference is the number of parties legally allowed to compete.

summary.questionText: Briefly describe Tanzania's transition to multipartyism.
summary.correctAnswer: Tanzania was a one-party state for many years, then amended its constitution in 1992 to allow more than one party, returning the country to multi-party democracy.
summary.explanation: The 1992 constitutional amendment is the central fact of the transition.

summary.questionText: State the role of the opposition in a democracy.
summary.correctAnswer: The opposition checks the government, criticises poor decisions, offers alternative policies and holds leaders accountable to the people.
summary.explanation: The opposition provides scrutiny, alternatives and accountability.

summary.questionText: Distinguish between a political party and a pressure group.
summary.correctAnswer: A political party seeks to form the government, while a pressure group only tries to influence government decisions on specific issues without forming a government.
summary.explanation: Parties want power; pressure groups want influence.

summary.questionText: Identify three examples of civil society organisations.
summary.correctAnswer: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs), trade unions and faith-based organisations.
summary.explanation: These independent groups all form part of civil society.

summary.questionText: Explain the role of the media in a democracy.
summary.correctAnswer: The media informs citizens, provides a platform for different views, and acts as a watchdog that exposes corruption and abuse of power.
summary.explanation: Information, a public platform and watchdog functions are the media's key democratic roles.

summary.questionText: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of a multi-party system.
summary.correctAnswer: Advantages: it gives citizens a choice of leaders and policies and allows peaceful change of power; disadvantage: it can create division and conflict if competition becomes too bitter.
summary.explanation: Choice and peaceful competition are strengths; division is a common weakness.

summary.questionText: Why is citizen participation important in a democracy?
summary.correctAnswer: Citizen participation ensures that government reflects the will of the people, keeps leaders accountable and strengthens democracy.
summary.explanation: Participation links the government to the people and supports accountability.

hoq.questionText: A country bans all parties except the ruling one and claims this makes the nation more united. Which statement best evaluates this argument?

options.text: It is fully correct because removing other parties always guarantees unity
It may reduce open competition, but it also limits citizens' choice and weakens accountability, so unity is not guaranteed
It has no effect on democracy at all

hoq.explanation: Banning other parties limits choice and weakens checks on the government, so claimed unity comes at the cost of accountability and may even hide discontent rather than remove it.

hoq.questionText: An NGO publishes a report exposing misuse of public funds, and a newspaper spreads the story. How do these actions strengthen democracy?

options.text: They replace the role of the courts and parliament
They act as watchdogs, informing the public and increasing pressure on leaders to be accountable
They form a new political party

hoq.explanation: Civil society and the media act as watchdogs; by informing citizens of wrongdoing they raise public pressure that pushes leaders toward accountability without replacing state institutions.

hoq.questionText: Two groups want change: one fields candidates to win the next election, the other only lobbies leaders to pass a new health law. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Both are political parties because both want change
The first is a political party seeking power, while the second is a pressure group seeking to influence policy
Both are pressure groups because neither uses elections
Neither has any role in a democracy

hoq.explanation: Contesting elections to gain power marks the first as a political party, while lobbying on a single issue without seeking to govern marks the second as a pressure group.
